questions.question: Heating a solid increases the AMPLITUDE of atomic vibration, not the atom size. Explain how that produces expansion.
questions.solution: Atoms vibrate about equilibrium in an asymmetric (anharmonic) potential: as amplitude grows, the average separation shifts outward because the repulsive wall steepens faster than the attractive side. Greater average spacing ⇒ the whole lattice expands. Expansion is a statistical shift of mean positions, not bigger atoms.

questions.question: Why is the area expansion coefficient β ≈ 2α and volume coefficient γ ≈ 3α?
questions.solution: Each linear dimension grows by (1 + αΔT); area grows by (1 + αΔT)² ≈ 1 + 2αΔT (dropping α²ΔT², tiny), so β = 2α. Volume: (1 + αΔT)³ ≈ 1 + 3αΔT, so γ = 3α. The relations hold for isotropic solids in the small-expansion limit.

questions.question: A metal plate with a circular hole is heated. Does the hole get bigger or smaller?
questions.solution: Bigger — every linear dimension, including the distance between any two points of the plate, scales up by the same factor. The hole behaves as if it were made of the same expanding material. (Cooling shrinks the hole — the opposite of what 'the metal contracts onto the hole' intuition says.)

questions.question: Why does a bimetallic strip of brass and iron bend when heated, and which way?
questions.solution: Brass expands more (larger α) than iron for the same temperature rise; the brass side becomes longer, so the strip curves with brass on the OUTSIDE of the curve. The differential expansion converts temperature into mechanical motion — the working principle of thermostats.

questions.question: Why does a lake freeze from the TOP down, and why does that matter for aquatic life?
questions.solution: Water has maximum density at 4 °C: cooling below 4 °C makes it EXPAND and float. So 4 °C water sinks and the surface reaches 0 °C first — ice forms on top and insulates the water below, which stays at ~4 °C. Fish survive because the densest water stays liquid at the bottom.

questions.question: A liquid in a metal vessel seems to expand less than its true coefficient. Explain what is happening.
questions.solution: The vessel expands too, enlarging the interior volume, so the measured rise is only the DIFFERENCE between real liquid expansion and vessel expansion: γ_apparent = γ_real − γ_vessel ≈ γ_real − 3α_metal. The liquid's true expansion is larger than what the stem shows. Real expansion needs the container's expansion corrected out.

questions.question: Above 4 °C water expands on heating as expected — but from 0 to 4 °C it CONTRACTS. Why, and why does this matter for lakes?
questions.solution: On melting, the hydrogen-bond network partly collapses and molecules pack closer, so heating 0–4 °C lets further structural rearrangement shrink the volume; above 4 °C thermal agitation dominates and normal expansion resumes. Consequently water at 4 °C is DENSEST and sinks, so a freezing lake keeps 4 °C water at the bottom while ice forms on the surface. Aquatic life survives because ice floats and is a poor conductor.

questions.question: Two thin strips of different metals riveted together curl when heated. Why is the bend systematic rather than random?
questions.solution: Each metal has a different linear expansivity, so for the same temperature change they want different new lengths. Being bonded, they must share one length, so the higher-expansivity metal stretches less than it wants and the lower one is forced to stretch more — producing a curvature. The strip bends TOWARD the lower-expansivity metal, because the longer-wanting side forms the outer arc. The bend direction is set predictably by which α is larger.
